q: What does this program print? (Elapsed time)
why: Elapsed time is the later reading minus the earlier one: 12.75 - 10.5 is 2.25.

q: What does this program print? (Sleep function)
code:
import time
from datetime import date, datetime, timedelta, timezone
import subprocess, shlex, sched, threading
print(time.sleep(0.01))
why: time.sleep waits and returns nothing, so print shows None.

q: What does this program print? (Monotonic clock)
code:
import time
from datetime import date, datetime, timedelta, timezone
import subprocess, shlex, sched, threading
print(time.get_clock_info('time').monotonic, time.get_clock_info('monotonic').monotonic)
why: time.time() reads the clock that can be set, so it is not monotonic; time.monotonic() is.

q: What does this program print? (Round function)
code: print(round(2.5), round(3.5), round(0.5))
why: round sends a half to the even neighbour, so 2.5 gives 2, 3.5 gives 4 and 0.5 gives 0.

q: What does this program print? (Epoch timestamp)
code:
import time
from datetime import date, datetime, timedelta, timezone
import subprocess, shlex, sched, threading
print(time.gmtime(86400)[:3])
why: The timestamp counts seconds from 1 January 1970 UTC; 86400 seconds is one day, so the date is 2 January 1970.

q: What does this program print? (Readable time string)
code:
import time
from datetime import date, datetime, timedelta, timezone
import subprocess, shlex, sched, threading
print(time.asctime(time.gmtime(0)))
why: Timestamp 0 is the epoch, a Thursday; the day of the month is padded to width 2 with a space, giving two spaces before the 1.

q: What does this program print? (Local versus utc)
code:
import time
from datetime import date, datetime, timedelta, timezone
import subprocess, shlex, sched, threading
print(datetime.fromtimestamp(1000000, timezone.utc).hour)
why: 1,000,000 seconds is 11 days, 13 hours, 46 minutes and 40 seconds after the epoch, so in UTC the hour is 13; a local zone would give another reading.

q: What does this program print? (Datetime object)
code:
import time
from datetime import date, datetime, timedelta, timezone
import subprocess, shlex, sched, threading
d = datetime(2026, 10, 21)
print(d.hour, datetime(2026, 10, 21, 16, 29).minute)
why: Hour, minute and second default to 0, so the first value is 0; the second datetime has minute 29.

q: What does this program print? (Current moment)
code:
import time
from datetime import date, datetime, timedelta, timezone
import subprocess, shlex, sched, threading
print(datetime.now().tzinfo)
why: datetime.now() with no zone argument returns a naive value, whose tzinfo is None.

q: What does this program print? (Datetime comparison)
code:
import time
from datetime import date, datetime, timedelta, timezone
import subprocess, shlex, sched, threading
print(datetime(2026, 10, 31) < datetime(2027, 1, 1), datetime(2026, 10, 31) == datetime(2026, 10, 31, 0, 0))
why: The earlier moment is the smaller one, and two datetimes with the same fields are equal.

q: What does this program print? (Timedelta object)
code:
import time
from datetime import date, datetime, timedelta, timezone
import subprocess, shlex, sched, threading
d = timedelta(hours=49)
print(d.days, d.seconds)
why: 49 hours normalise into 2 days and 3600 seconds (1 hour).

q: What does this program print? (Duration readouts)
code:
import time
from datetime import date, datetime, timedelta, timezone
import subprocess, shlex, sched, threading
print(timedelta(days=1, hours=2).total_seconds())
why: One day is 86400 seconds and two hours 7200; total_seconds returns the sum as a float.

q: What does this program print? (Duration units)
code:
import time
from datetime import date, datetime, timedelta, timezone
import subprocess, shlex, sched, threading
print(timedelta(weeks=1, hours=24).days)
why: A week is 7 days and 24 hours is one more day, so the days attribute is 8.

q: What does this program print? (Add subtract duration)
code:
import time
from datetime import date, datetime, timedelta, timezone
import subprocess, shlex, sched, threading
print(datetime(2028, 2, 28) + timedelta(days=1))
why: 2028 is a leap year, so the day after 28 February is 29 February; print shows the date and time.

q: What does this program print? (Date difference)
code:
import time
from datetime import date, datetime, timedelta, timezone
import subprocess, shlex, sched, threading
print(date(2027, 1, 1) - date(2026, 10, 31))
why: Subtracting two dates gives a timedelta: from 31 October to 1 January is 30 + 31 + 1 = 62 days, and str shows the clock part.

q: What does this program print? (Weekday of date)
code:
import time
from datetime import date, datetime, timedelta, timezone
import subprocess, shlex, sched, threading
d = date(2019, 1, 7)
print(d.weekday(), d.strftime('%A'))
why: 7 January 2019 was a Monday; weekday() counts Monday as 0.

q: What does this program print? (Strftime format)
code:
import time
from datetime import date, datetime, timedelta, timezone
import subprocess, shlex, sched, threading
print(datetime(2026, 10, 21, 16, 29).strftime('%I:%M %p'))
why: %I is the 12-hour clock padded to two digits and %p gives AM or PM; 16:29 is 04:29 PM.

q: What does this program print? (Strptime parse)
code:
import time
from datetime import date, datetime, timedelta, timezone
import subprocess, shlex, sched, threading
print(datetime.strptime('21/10/2026', '%d/%m/%Y').month)
why: The format reads the day first, then the month, so the month is 10.

q: What does this program print? (Two digit year)
code:
import time
from datetime import date, datetime, timedelta, timezone
import subprocess, shlex, sched, threading
print([datetime.strptime(s, '%y').year for s in ('68', '69')])
why: %y maps 69 to 99 to 1969 to 1999 and 0 to 68 to 2000 to 2068.

q: What does this program print? (Parse mismatch)
code:
import time
from datetime import date, datetime, timedelta, timezone
import subprocess, shlex, sched, threading
try:
    datetime.strptime('2026-10-21', '%Y/%m/%d')
except ValueError:
    print('ValueError')
why: The text uses hyphens where the format has slashes, so strptime raises ValueError.

q: What does this program print? (Naive versus aware)
code:
import time
from datetime import date, datetime, timedelta, timezone
import subprocess, shlex, sched, threading
print(datetime(2026, 1, 1) == datetime(2026, 1, 1, tzinfo=timezone.utc))
why: A naive and an aware datetime are never equal (equality gives False, while ordering raises TypeError).

q: What does this program print? (Utcnow deprecated)
code:
import time
from datetime import date, datetime, timedelta, timezone
import subprocess, shlex, sched, threading
print(datetime.now(timezone.utc).tzinfo)
why: The value made with a UTC zone is aware; its tzinfo prints as UTC. This is the replacement for the deprecated utcnow().

q: What does this program print? (Yearless parsing)
code:
import time
from datetime import date, datetime, timedelta, timezone
import subprocess, shlex, sched, threading
print(datetime.strptime('02/29;1984', '%m/%d;%Y').date())
why: With a leap year in the text and the format, 29 February parses; without a year Python would use 1900, which has no 29 February.

q: What does this program print? (Run function)
code:
import time
from datetime import date, datetime, timedelta, timezone
import subprocess, shlex, sched, threading
print(subprocess.CompletedProcess(['calc.exe'], 0))
why: A CompletedProcess shows its arguments and return code.

q: What does this program print? (Argument list)
code:
import time
from datetime import date, datetime, timedelta, timezone
import subprocess, shlex, sched, threading
print(shlex.split("notepad 'my file.txt'"))
why: shlex.split keeps a quoted name with a space as one argument.

q: What does this program print? (Capture output)
code:
import time
from datetime import date, datetime, timedelta, timezone
import subprocess, shlex, sched, threading
p = subprocess.CompletedProcess(['x'], 0, stdout='hi\n')
print(repr(p.stdout))
why: With text output the stdout attribute is a string that keeps the newline; repr makes the newline visible.

q: What does this program print? (Exit code)
code:
import time
from datetime import date, datetime, timedelta, timezone
import subprocess, shlex, sched, threading
p = subprocess.CompletedProcess(['x'], 3)
try:
    p.check_returncode()
except subprocess.CalledProcessError:
    print('failed', p.returncode)
why: A nonzero return code makes check_returncode raise CalledProcessError.

q: What does this program print? (Poll and wait)
code:
import time
from datetime import date, datetime, timedelta, timezone
import subprocess, shlex, sched, threading
print([m for m in ('poll', 'wait', 'kill', 'sleep') if hasattr(subprocess.Popen, m)])
why: Popen objects have poll, wait and kill; sleep is a function of the time module, not a method of a process.

q: What does this program print? (Shell true)
code:
import time
from datetime import date, datetime, timedelta, timezone
import subprocess, shlex, sched, threading
print(shlex.quote('a b'))
why: shlex.quote wraps text with a space in single quotes so a shell reads it as one word.

q: What does this program print? (Sched module)
code:
import time
from datetime import date, datetime, timedelta, timezone
import subprocess, shlex, sched, threading
log, clock = [], [0]
s = sched.scheduler(lambda: clock[0], lambda d: clock.__setitem__(0, clock[0] + d))
s.enter(5, 1, log.append, ('five',))
s.enter(2, 1, log.append, ('two',))
s.run()
print(log)
why: The scheduler runs events in the order of their time, not the order they were entered.

q: What does this program print? (Timer thread)
code:
import time
from datetime import date, datetime, timedelta, timezone
import subprocess, shlex, sched, threading
print(issubclass(threading.Timer, threading.Thread))
why: threading.Timer is a subclass of Thread: it waits in a thread of its own.

q: What does this program print? (Lap timing)
code:
marks = [0, 3.56, 8.63, 17.68]
print([round(b - a, 2) for a, b in zip(marks, marks[1:])])
why: Each lap is the difference between consecutive marks; the totals are the marks themselves.

q: What does this program print? (Prettified laps)
code: print('Lap #' + str(1).rjust(2) + ':')
why: rjust(2) pads the 1 on the left with one space to width 2.

q: What does this program print? (Interrupt to stop)
code: print(issubclass(KeyboardInterrupt, Exception), issubclass(KeyboardInterrupt, BaseException))
why: KeyboardInterrupt derives from BaseException only, so 'except Exception' does not catch it.

q: What does this program print? (Countdown loop)
code: print(list(range(3, 0, -1)))
why: The range counts down from 3 and stops before 0.

q: What does this program print? (Time until event)
code:
import time
from datetime import date, datetime, timedelta, timezone
import subprocess, shlex, sched, threading
print(datetime(2027, 1, 1) - datetime(2026, 10, 1, 12))
why: From noon on 1 October to midnight on 1 January is 91 days and 12 hours.

q: What does this program print? (Forward search)
code:
import time
from datetime import date, datetime, timedelta, timezone
import subprocess, shlex, sched, threading
d = date(2026, 10, 1)
found = []
while len(found) < 2:
    d += timedelta(days=1)
    if d.day == 13 and d.weekday() == 4:
        found.append(d.isoformat())
print(found)
why: The next two Fridays that fall on the 13th after 1 October 2026 are 13 November 2026 and 13 August 2027.

q: What does this program print? (Backward search)
code:
import time
from datetime import date, datetime, timedelta, timezone
import subprocess, shlex, sched, threading
try:
    date.min - timedelta(days=1)
except OverflowError:
    print('OverflowError')
why: date.min is 1 January of year 1; one day earlier is outside the supported range.

q: Which statement about the number returned by time.time() is correct?
options: It is the number of milliseconds since the program started
It is the local date written as one integer
It is the number of seconds since 1 January 1970 at 00:00 UTC, as a float
It is the number of seconds since midnight today
why: time.time() returns seconds since the epoch, midnight UTC on 1 January 1970.

q: What does time.sleep(2) do?
options: It schedules the next line to run in two seconds while the program goes on
It stops the program after two seconds
It runs the next line two times
It blocks the calling program for at least two seconds without using processor time
why: time.sleep suspends the calling thread for at least the time given.

q: Why is time.monotonic() preferred over time.time() for timing a block of code?
options: Its readings never go backwards, even if someone sets the system clock
It returns whole seconds, which are easier to subtract
It returns the date as well as the time
It is faster because it does not read the clock
why: A monotonic clock is not affected by changes of the system clock.

q: Why can the same timestamp print different clock readings on two computers?
options: The timestamp counts seconds differently on each system
Each computer converts it to its own local time zone
why: datetime.fromtimestamp without a zone gives local time, so the zone decides the reading.

q: What replaces datetime.utcnow(), deprecated since Python 3.12?
options: datetime.today(), which returns a UTC date
datetime.now(datetime.UTC), which returns an aware value
why: utcnow returns a naive value that looks like local time; an aware UTC value avoids that confusion.

q: What does the zoneinfo module give a datetime?
options: A fixed offset from UTC that never changes
The current weather at the zone
A time zone from the IANA database, with its daylight saving rules, as its tzinfo
why: ZoneInfo('America/Los_Angeles') knows when the offset changes.

q: What happens when one day is added to an aware datetime in a zone just before daylight saving time starts?
options: The wall-clock reading moves one day, although the elapsed time is 23 hours
The result is the same moment
why: Arithmetic on an aware datetime in one zone moves the wall clock, not the elapsed time.

q: What does subprocess.run(args, check=True) do when the program exits with a nonzero code?
options: It returns the exit code as the text of an error
why: check=True turns a failure code into an exception; timeout raises TimeoutExpired instead.

q: How does subprocess.Popen differ from subprocess.run?
options: Popen waits for the program, run does not
Popen can only run Python programs
Popen returns at once while the program keeps running; run waits until it ends
run starts the program in a separate window
why: Popen gives an object for the running process so the program can continue alongside it.

q: What does the kill() method of a Popen object do?
options: It asks the program politely to close and waits
It ends the process at once, so unsaved work in it is lost
why: kill sends a forceful stop; terminate asks more gently on some systems.

q: How does a program open a document in its default application on macOS?
options: It runs the open command with the file name as an argument
It calls time.sleep with the file name
why: On Windows the start command is used (with shell=True), on macOS open, on many Linux systems xdg-open.

q: What does webbrowser.open(url) return?
options: True if a browser was launched
The status code of the page
why: webbrowser.open starts the default browser and reports whether it could.

q: Why is the operating system's scheduler (cron, launchd, Task Scheduler) used instead of a Python loop that sleeps?
options: It can start the program at chosen times even when no Python program is running
It does not need a program to run
why: A sleeping Python program must stay running; the system scheduler does not.

q: Which module of the chapter reads the system clock and pauses a program?
why: The time module has time(), ctime(), monotonic() and sleep().

q: Which module holds moments and durations as datetime and timedelta values?
why: datetime provides date, datetime and timedelta; zoneinfo only adds IANA time zones to them.

q: Which standard-library module starts another program from Python?
why: subprocess.run and subprocess.Popen start other programs; webbrowser and shlex only help with browsers and command text.

q: What is the difference between an operating-system scheduler and the sched module?
options: They are the same tool under two names
sched starts programs at boot; the system scheduler only runs functions
The system scheduler starts programs even when none of yours is running; sched runs functions inside one running program
The system scheduler works inside one program; sched works across all programs
why: cron, launchd and Task Scheduler belong to the operating system; sched.scheduler is a library object.

q: What do the chapter's three projects (stopwatch, countdown, Friday the 13th finder) have in common?
options: Each is built from clock readings and durations: subtraction of times and loops over them
why: All three combine time or datetime values with timedelta arithmetic and a loop.

q: Which pair of functions measures a stretch of time and pauses a program?
options: time.monotonic() or time.perf_counter() to measure, and time.sleep() to pause
time.sleep() to measure and time.time() to pause
datetime.now() to pause and time.sleep() to measure
sched.run() to measure and subprocess.run() to pause
why: The monotonic clocks give readings to subtract; sleep blocks for at least the given seconds.

q: What are the two forms in which the time module reports the current moment in the chapter?
options: A datetime object and a timedelta
A float count of seconds since the epoch and a text from ctime()
A list of year, month and day only
A string of hours only and an integer of days only
why: time.time() gives the count and time.ctime() gives readable text in local time.

q: What makes one datetime greater than another?
options: It has more digits in its year
It was created later in the program
It has a longer printed text
why: Comparison operators order datetimes by the moment they stand for.

q: Which units can a timedelta be built from?
options: Weeks, days, hours, minutes, seconds, milliseconds and microseconds
why: Months and years have no fixed length, so timedelta does not accept them.

q: What does subtracting one datetime from another give?
why: datetime minus datetime is a timedelta; datetime plus or minus a timedelta is a datetime.

q: Which pair converts a datetime to text and text to a datetime?
options: strptime and strftime, in the same order
why: strftime formats (datetime to text); strptime parses (text to datetime).

q: Why can a naive datetime not be compared in order with an aware one?
options: Python converts both to UTC and compares them without any problem
The naive one is always the earlier
They do not say which moment they stand for in the same way, so Python raises TypeError
Both are equal when their fields match
why: Equality between naive and aware gives False, but ordering raises TypeError.

q: What does subprocess.run return?
options: A Popen object for a running process
The process id as an integer
A CompletedProcess with the arguments, the return code and, if captured, the output
why: run waits for the program to end and returns a CompletedProcess.

q: Which methods let a program check, wait for and end a process started with Popen?
why: poll returns None while the process runs; wait blocks; kill ends it at once.

q: What is the risk of subprocess.run(text, shell=True) with text from outside?
options: The program runs more slowly but safely
The text is run by the system shell, so it can carry extra commands unless it is quoted
why: shlex.quote protects outside text; a list of arguments avoids the shell.

q: Which of these can start a program at a chosen time even when your Python program is not running?
options: The operating system's scheduler (Task Scheduler, launchd, cron)
why: sleep, sched and Timer all need a running Python program.

q: How does the stopwatch compute the time of one lap?
options: It subtracts the start time from now
It adds the last two laps
It reads a clock that counts laps
It subtracts the time of the last lap from the time now
why: The total is now minus the start; the lap is now minus the last lap.

q: How does the countdown program wait between prints?
options: It sleeps one second, then subtracts one from the seconds left
It runs a loop that checks the clock without sleeping
It starts a new process each second
It adds one second to a timedelta
why: time.sleep(1) pauses without using processor time.

q: What two conditions must a date meet for the Friday the 13th finders?
options: The month is 13 and the weekday is 4
The day of the month is 13 and the weekday is Friday
The day is 5 and the weekday is 13
why: date.day == 13 and date.weekday() == 4 (Monday is 0).
